text_fidelity_a:
Lowepro Passport Sling DSLR Camera Bag I was looking for a sling camera bag for ease of use when I am in action mode, e.g., hanging off the side of a jeep during safari, hanging over the railing of a boat while photographing breaching whales. I did not want the typical backpack or the shoulder bag (both of which I own) that would impede me from such movements and/or would need to be set down while I was shooting.

I like to leave my zoom lens on my camera. I attach a lens in the open as few times as possible for the obvious reasons, e.g., salt air, dust. I have a Nikon 200-500 lens attached to a D4 body. With that configuration, the camera/lens is 14.25" long, D4 body is 6" wide and lens at its widest is 5" and it fills this bag's length (including the unzipped 30% extra). That set up is also about 10-11 pounds of weight. However, in order to fit it . . . I had to remove the square cushioned "cube" that is affixed by velcro into one side of the bag. Once my cameras/lens was in the bag, there was about 3" of horizontal (lengthwise space) left and 3" of vertical space as well as small pockets of space around the camera/lens itself. I would not be able to fit my IPad. I could probably tuck my IPhone in somewhere. Extra batteries, battery charger and cords would be doubtful. One extra battery perhaps.

The zipper on the top can be zipped either way (which I like). There are cords on the zippers as well for easy grabbing. The "open" pockets on the outside are nice, and while they are 6" deep, there isn't much that has any value that I would store there . . . because the risk of it falling out would be too great. (At least for me . . . because I plan to sling the sling quite a bit). It is difficult to believe that the inside of this bag only has 2 very small pockets. Both pockets have flaps that velcro. One pocket is 4"d x 3"w and the other is 4"d x 2"w. While that seems like a lot . . . the pockets are sewn into the bag and some of that width is lost to the stitching. They are immediately adjacent to each other and immediately under the top zipper (not the most optimum place to be IMHO).

The strap is nice and sturdy and reminds me of my Nikon strap. What I also like is that instead of having the typical strap tightener (don't recall the technical term, but like a buckle), this strap has a cam lock buckle. It is a buckle clip that clips down with pressure on the strap. It will take you less time to adjust your strap, which might not be a big deal to some . . . if you don't adjust your strap very often. Loaded it down with approximately 12 pounds of equipment, slung it on my back and tested it by moving around for a while today . . . and it stayed put. Hopefully, it will do the same when in the field. Strap has 6" wide removable cushion that velcros into place. I will probably double that with another one to make it super comfy. I am 6'0" tall. With the strap over my left shoulder (and the bag sitting on my right hip) and the strap completely extended . . . the top of the bag (where it zips open), is approximately 25" vertically from my right shoulder.

Canvas feels heavyweight. It feels like it might be waxed (and therefore water resistant), but after a bit of due diligence, I cannot find anything that would confirm same. But, you could sling this over your shoulder under a rain jacket or poncho if necessary.

The color is just right for safari (bright colors, whites, greys and/or blacks are frowned upon). This is the main reason why I did not purchase the Passport II or III . . . no natural color choices.

I would describe myself as an intermediate amateur photographer and it has become my hobby in retirement. I live for nature action shots.

I am keeping this bag. I am going to cut off one side of the cushioned "cube" to make a cushioned "U". The open end of the "U" will face up. I will place the camera in the bag so that the cushioned U will cradle my large lens with my camera attached. While it doesn't hold as much as I would like . . . I liken it to a wristlet wallet. It holds exactly what I need at the time I need it. I will still have my camera backpack with me (to hold extra batteries, lenses and the like) and my hubby usually volunteers for carry duty - lucky me! I would like to have given it 5 stars . . . but I feel as though the design needs improvement (the II and III are about the same in size etc.). Unfortunately, this also seems to be the only true sling bag on the market. (My definition of sling is worn like a crossbody with the bag on your back instead of in front).

Look forward to breaking it in very soon.
text_fidelity_b: Lowepro Passport Sling DSLR Camera Bag

text_fidelity_a:
HP ENVY Desktop Computer, Intel Core i7-10700, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB Hard Drive & 512 GB SSD Storage, Windows 10 Pro (TE01-1254, 2020 Model) It is an alright system if you are only going to be doing basic computing like Microsoft Office, email, and some Netflix (but maybe not all at the same time). However, at a current price of over $850 being saddle with only the onboard graphics is hardly acceptable. Second, this system is also only okay if you never plan to repair the computer if there are issues with the power supply or motherboard. If you toss out your systems when they break, then this will work. If you like to swap out the bad parts, run for the hills you do not want to be stuck dealing with the HP part store.

If you want to play any games or use programs that require a bit more heavy lifting, (design software, CAD, or anything pulling a bunch of images or rendering) or need to have several programs running at once, you are going to struggle without a graphics card.

But can't you just add your own Graphics Card, I mean it is 2020 after all? Well... while this system does have an open slot on the motherboard for the addition of a graphics card it is severely handicapped in using it. For one, it is a very small case and you will be stuck with a small form factor card, which tend to be more expensive than their standard size counterparts. Worse yet, the included system power is only 180 watts. You cannot run much past whatever is already in the system with that, so you will need to also upgrade the power supply. Here is where it gets annoying. HP not only uses their own motherboard (Baker in this system) but the motherboard uses a proprietary connection to the power supply, so you HAVE TO BUY their power supply and only theirs. There is not an adapter, I looked and looked and looked some more.

That means heading over to the HP parts store website and trying not to pound your head into a wall with how backwards and outdated their system is. If you manage to locate the ONLY 400 watt power supply that works with the baker motherboard (yes 400 watt is the biggest they make that work for this case and motherboard) you will be hit with a $125 price tag (more like $150 after tax and shipping) for a power supply that should really cost half that. Which even if it says is in stock, will likely be back-ordered. They told me I'd be lucky to see it in 2 months even if it says "instock" in the system. Because they are the only ones selling it, you have to either wait or just forget about the upgrade. If you NEED it because your current power supply isn't working, well too bad for you.

If you have hung in this far and managed to get the power supply squared away, you can start on the graphics card piece. Now here is where it gets fun, you will want to avoid the HP parts store. They have the GTX 1660ti listed but its price bounces from over $1000 (yes a grand) to around $700 for a card that is about $300 on Amazon. Due to the power supply limitations a 1660ti is as high as you are going to be able to get, which puts you on par with an entry level gaming laptop. Due to size limitations of the HP Envy case you will want to stick to a small form factor card (generally that means one fan not two, but measure first some of those single fans are still a bit long).

So between the $150 power supply (that you may never get) and the ($300 graphics card off amazon) you are looking at about $450 in an upgrade to basically keep pace with a low level gaming laptop that costs less than what you paid for the HP Envy to begin with.

Which is my biggest problem with this system and the reason for the 3 stars, because it only does what it says (so earns its 3 stars) BUT if it has any sort of hardware issue down the line or doesn't meet your needs, you are going to be stuck buying a whole new system or be left to the mercy of HPs terribly unreliable part store with its over inflated prices and unreliable delivery timetables.
text_fidelity_b: HP ENVY Desktop Computer, Intel Core i7-10700, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB Hard Drive & 512 GB SSD Storage, Windows 10 Pro (TE01-1254, 2020 Model)

text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell 3 – enhanced wifi, improved motion detection, easy installation Great wireless camera/doorbell. Hardware/software this is ideal. We live on a busy street so we were getting lots of notifications. The software allowed us to adjust where the camera sensed motion, cutting down "false" notifications. Easy to use.
Easy to setup and install. Took maybe 15 minutes from opening the box to having it up and running.
Convenient set-up and access via phone (iOS and Android) app. Added skill to Echo, so when someone sets of camera or pushes doorbell, we get a notification via Alexa, and an image on the Echo show. You can adjust how often and what notifications you receive in the app.
Night vision is pretty good as well. Another nice feature is you can access a "live" view anytime, notification or not.
Audio works well, so if you are in the basement, garage, at work, shopping you can talk to whomever is at your door.
If you carry your phone everywhere or have a smart home speaker (Google, Echo or maybe Apple?) you won't need the additional chime, phone and speakers have a decently loud sound.
I would suggest getting a second battery if you have a busy street or lots of activity. The app notifies you in plenty of time the battery is low and needs to be recharged (only takes a couple hours to fully charge). But a second battery extends the life and less work (but to be fair, one screw using included driver, slide off plate, slide battery out, set to charge and reverse process to put battery back in. With two batteries, the whole thing takes about two minutes. With one, you simply have a non-functioning doorbell/camera for a few hours. No biggie, just FYI.
Also there is an an App called Neighbors free to join and use. It lets you share "videos and notifications of criminal or suspicious activity. So if someone in your neighborhood is broken into or home is vandalized they can share the video and/or share a notice of the incident. Lost dog, share. Delivery thieves, share. So both kinda cool and scary.
Now the BAD. To access the video you have to pay a monthly fee ( now if you access the video within the first 30 seconds or so, you are golden, but if you have your hands full, or can't access your phone, you can't see the video, or back it up. While the basic few is like $40 ish a year. Higher for the next tier up. That is forever. And no easy way to back up to a local storage device. All files are on Rings servers.
Now if you know that up front, and $40 is no biggie. Then 5 stars.
But for me that is an issue.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell 3 – enhanced wifi, improved motion detection, easy installation

Gosky 12x55 High Definition Monocular Telescope and Quick Smartphone Holder - 2018 This is a really nice optical device. I hadn't necessarily heard of Gosky before, but I gather they are a big brand in optics. I'm also going on relatively little education on the subject that a monocular is easier to focus at longer distances and/or a larger range of distances because you don't have to focus the two lenses - something which makes it hard for me to look through binoculars after a while.

This is pretty lightweight, but feels very solid and nice. It has a turn-out piece to the rear of the rear lens to accommodate people who don't wear glasses. And besides that, there is only one knob to turn to focus, mostly depending on the distance to the object of your attention.

The carry case is fairly rugged nylon and has a belt loop, but not the kind of belt loop you can use without unstrapping your belt. It's also a little large for a belt in my opinion, but may come in handy. The hand strap is pretty nice, but there is a lot of extra length to the strap I really don't know what to do with, and I feel like the actual attachment process could be more refined. I do really like that both lens covers can stay attached to the body while not in use (rear one can be attached to the hand strap and front on is attached to a rubber ring which stays on the body) which makes for a refined and complete product.

Not sure if this one can accommodate a cell phone holder or not...seems like people must take pictures through these things when birding or spying or watching opera or whatever they're doing.

Nice product. I now have a good feeling about this brand that was previously off my radar.
text_fidelity_b: Gosky 12x55 High Definition Monocular Telescope and Quick Smartphone Holder - 2018

You can still remove the grippy squares one, but the grippy stuff won't re-attach as well once all the dust in the air gets to it.

Additionally, the sliding on and off touches your screen. you can't really do it on an active screen without out potentially messing up what you are working on. I could touch through it, but not as well as without it. But the fact that it is touching your screen somewhere all the time caused a lot of issues just trying to type or click on something. The touches moved the cursor all over the place. So not really useful on a touchscreen. And the product will work fine on a non-touchscreen.

CORSAIR Hydro Series H105 AIO Liquid CPU Cooler, 240mm Thick Radiator, Dual 120mm PWM Fans I've wanted to try one of these liquid CPU coolers for ages, but it always been a little too cheap to spend the extra money on one, and I confess I've been mildly concerned about using a liquid anything inside my computer. I'm glad I tried this out.

This particular model has a radiator style grate which the fan sits on (there is some conductive paste included), then has tubes leading to the cooler unit. The water is totally enclosed in the system, and I can see no danger of leakage. The fan is quiet and unobtrusive.

It has a four pin connector, so if your computer has a four pin connector as well, your computer can control the speed of the fan. However, the four pin connector can also connect to a three pin connector and it works fine, you just lose that extra bit of control.

The one small improvement I'd like to see is that the water/cooling area only goes to one side of the radiator type grate, not around all of the edges, so one side of it will always be hotter than the other. It still disperses heat well, just seems like a less efficient system then it could be.

Lastly, I love the thumbscrews included for installing. I hate dealing with normal screws, and the thumbscrews are such a thoughtful touch that it made me think well of the company for including them.

Overall, if you've been on the fence about testing out one of these new liquid CPU coolers, I don't see any reason not to try out this one. The price is reasonable for what it is, and it looks like a highly effective setup, certainly better than just using a fan.
text_fidelity_b: CORSAIR Hydro Series H105 AIO Liquid CPU Cooler, 240mm Thick Radiator, Dual 120mm PWM Fans

WiFi Video Projector, WEWATCH V10B Wireless Portable Movie Projector with Bluetooth Full HD 1080P Supported Home Theater Video Projector Compatible with HDMI, VGA, TV Stick, iPhone, Android The WEWATCH V30 Portable Projector is a good 1080p projector for its size. I watched some movies with the screen setup to 80-90 inches and the picture looked very good in a dark room. It's important to watch this projector in low ambient lighting due to its low ANSI lumens, as bright light will wash out the picture.

The size of the projector is not as small as the pictures make it seem. Though it is not advertised as a pico projector, I expected it to be smaller. With that said, the projector is not so large that it would be hard to transport or store when not in use.

Unfortunately, I was not able to get the Wi-Fi feature to work with my Iphone. This is not a dealbreaker for me, as I plugged a Roku stick into the HDMI port and the system worked well.

I was surprised by how good the native speakers sound. I found watching movies enjoyable and voices were easy to hear. There are adjustments for the bass and treble levels in the menus. The unit has a headphone jack in the rear which makes hooking up an external speaker set up a breeze.

The fan on the unit is very quiet and is not distracting while it is in use.

While I really like this projector, there is a large downside. The lack of keystone correction is a huge oversight. Placing this projector without keystone adjustment means the projector has to be directly in line with the viewing area making it necessary to use a tripod in most instances. Having to bring a tripod along, makes the unit less portable.

Overall, this is a small projector with a great picture, as long as you can place it in the perfect location without much ambient lighting. If WEWATCH added keystone correction and refined the mirroring feature, this would be a 5 star projector.
text_fidelity_b: WiFi Video Projector, WEWATCH V10B Wireless Portable Movie Projector with Bluetooth Full HD 1080P Supported Home Theater Video Projector Compatible with HDMI, VGA, TV Stick, iPhone, Android

text_fidelity_a: Swimbuds Sport Premium Waterproof Headphones & 11 eartips in 4 Styles (Upgraded Cord) This is my second pair of Swimbuds. I've always struggled finding headphones that would not leak while swimming.  It must be some anatomical issue with my ear canal, because I've tried at least a dozen headphones - and all of them leaked or fell out at some point.  These swim buds are so light that they actually stay in my ear.  Short cord doesn't get tangled up.  And I guess the Christmas-tree tips are a bit different because so far these headphones are the only one that have not leaked, but I do have to insert them deep into ear canal.  I use just a touch of petroleum jelly on tips to help the insertion and to moisturise ears, because these headphones (like most other waterproof headphones) can cause irritation of the external ear canal.  There are a lot of tips to choose from.  I use them in my Endless Pool, so I don't know how they will perform in regular pool during turns and flips, but my guess is because of their lightness they will work fine.  I don't care much for clarity of music during swimming, but I found sound to be quite acceptable with these headphones.

Samsung Galaxy 5.0 Android MP3 Player Pros: Bought one of these refurbished for my 10 year old son. I read a terrible review on Cnet and man is it wrong. Cons: None

Other Thoughts: This is a great player and is not a true tablet or phone and should not be compared to either, yet it can function as a tablet, movie player or even as a phone. Plus, it is a great gaming device and best of all, no iTunes to mess with. Set it as a mass storage device and off it goes. Also, It is a great ereader. FYI,the CPU is single core but plenty fast. The video gpu is faster than the iPod 4's. If you like Galaxy Phones you will like this a lot. I am not sure what motivated the Cnet review I read, but it was terrible.

text_fidelity_a:
NYNE Multimedia Inc Cruiser Portable Bluetooth Speaker (Grey/Green) Although there are a lot of positive points to be said about this product, a major flaw with it is that - even on low volumes and on songs without much bass - you can hear a bit of distortion, like crackly static, that sounds like a speaker that you're either working too hard or is at the end of its life. This becomes worse as the battery gets low. I consider this issue to be "understandable and sort of acceptable" considering the whole system has to run on battery power and most people aren't expecting high power out of such a setup. They might just have a high-pass crossover set too high to conserve power, and too much is cut off, resulting in messy sound.

When you charge your phone with the speaker's battery (which in itself is sort of a nice, if cannibalistic, feature, one that other devices claim even though it is inherent to the device; with this, the USB-A port was added specifically for this purpose), it lowers the volume to level 8 (there is nothing to tell you what level you're at) to keep from draining the battery quickly. Even at this medium level and below, this problem can be recognized.

The bike mounts are 4" apart, center to center, so make sure you have room on your bike handlebars if that is your purpose for ordering. Included bike mounts are good. It also comes with a neoprene case, a USB cable, and an audio cable, both red. With all these extras trying to give the appearance of premium, it doesn't actually come with a charger, not that this will be an issue for most people (you probably already have more than you know what to do with).

There should be keyhole slots built into the bike mounts so it could also be hung on the wall and removed easily, making it more versatile.

The unit pairs easily and immediately with my Blackberry every time, and it can control the tracks through the BT connection as well. It looks well made and has a good feel to it. It looks like it could almost be waterproof, although I noticed no mention or claim of that feature (so I'm sure it's not).

The sound overall isn't bad for a low voltage battery operated speaker, as long as you're not sitting down and listening too closely. I guess for the purposes of making noise as you ride around the neighborhood, it'll do just fine.
text_fidelity_b: NYNE Multimedia Inc Cruiser Portable Bluetooth Speaker (Grey/Green)

text_fidelity_a:
Sony ICFS79W AM/FM/Weather Band Digital Tuner Shower Radio (White) FM reception is flat out horrible where I live. It's like a radeo dead zone. My home theater system can pull in nothing. My stereo gets a lot of static. I listen almost exclusively online but I'd heard good things about this radio so I decided to give it a try. The reception was amazing. Perfectly clear. No static on FM at all. It sounds beautiful. The weather feed was full of static, but servicable--I ususally can't pull in the weather band at all. AM is average--neither the worse I've heard nor the best. But then, I don't expect much from AM.

It does the FM1, FM2 trick that some cars do. There is no difference. It just lets them repurpose the buttons. I find it odd, but not bad.

The only think I would have changed is how it hangs. If you don't have a shower hook (I don't) it hangs over the shower head. That tilts the entire unit forward. It should either suspend from the shower curtain rack (the strap is oriented the wrong way to do that--it would try to hand perpendicular to the curtain) or reach a better balance point. That's an issue of aesthetics, not function. I'd be worried about sitting it on the edge of the tub, as it is too likely to fall.

The one trick to remember, when sticking the antenna to the shower wall, is that suction cups don't work as well on a wet surface. Thoroughly dry the wall first, then place it. It helps will the issue of the antenna falling.
text_fidelity_b: Sony ICFS79W AM/FM/Weather Band Digital Tuner Shower Radio (White)

Powered USB Hub Rosonway 16 Ports 100W USB 3.0 Data Hub Aluminum USB Hub 3.0 Splitter with 12V/8.3A UL Certified Power Adapter and Individual On/Off Switches RSH-A16 (Black) I haven't yet used it to its full potential. The maximum ports I've used at one time was 5, but it worked well. I've heard others say it gets hot, which may be true if it is full and all in use, but so far, it has worked fine for me.

Speed seems to be consistent with USB 3 ports. It actually seems to be limited by the external drives I was using. I've been trying to go through my old 2.0 backup drives to make sure they are backed up on newer drives after I lost a number of older drives recently. These drives were expectedly slower than my newer drives. I eventually want to turn my computer into something of a backup server, including videos and other large files, so this will come in really handy.

I also like that you can turn on and off the power to drives as they are needed, by pushing an on/off button for each port, or you can leave them all on if needed. Because it is powered, it does not turn off power to the ports if the computer is restarted. For my use, it is perfect.

Update 7/20/22
Running 4 external drives on it has it very hot. Makes me a little nervous. The area under it is not very hot. It is currently sitting on carpet that can handle a bit of heat. And actually the base isn't too hot, just the sides. I've been running recovery of hard drives and backups using it and it has been in pretty steady use for a few days. I don't think I would recommend this in any environment where your computer is constantly on.
text_fidelity_b: Powered USB Hub Rosonway 16 Ports 100W USB 3.0 Data Hub Aluminum USB Hub 3.0 Splitter with 12V/8.3A UL Certified Power Adapter and Individual On/Off Switches RSH-A16 (Black)

—Battery life as advertised, lasts around 19 hours.

—On/Off slide switch rather than a button.
—Volume control.
—Noise cancellation.
—Sleek, modern, attractive design.

A Few Negatives:

—Single button for play/pause, forward and back, and nothing is labeled.

Overall, a good value for the money.

text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR Cable Modem CM500 - Compatible with all Cable Providers incl. Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox | For Cable Plans up to 400Mbps | DOCSIS 3.0 Comcast has repeatedly lied to me, sending me letters and alerts telling me that I need a new cable modem or my service will be seriously degraded. One time they went so far as to set a date when my service would NO longer work at all! Of course, I would never believe them without double-checking for myself, and I found out it was indeed an outright lie. Even the oldest DOCSIS versions can handle more than my 30Mbps connection. I suppose the lie was because they want me to rent their modem for $10 or more a month and relinquish control of my own network to them.

That said, it makes sense to upgrade when convenient to be sure you're future proofed. Eventually even the cheapest Internet plans will be upgraded to higher speeds. When I heard that I could register this on Comcast's network online without having to call them (and have them speak extremely condescendingly to me even though I'm a Systems Engineer), I was sold. Worth doing.

Note that just because DOCSIS 3.0 can reach speeds of 10Gbps with maxed out number of channels, this modem is 680Mbps, which will be out of date eventually, when we finally get Gigabit Ethernet to residences.

Another (of a million) thing(s) I hate about Comcast is that they by default use your AP (that they rent to you as part of a router/AP/modem combo) to create a public (virtual) wireless AP for their other customers. They say this will not affect your bandwidth, but it can affect your throughput. And it uses your electricity. And why would you want to help Comcast, when they take advantage of you any chance they can.

Point of all this is me encouraging you to get your own modem, get your own router and AP (or combo unit, although I prefer them separate) and pare down your ISP bill as much as you can. Stop giving them money.

Note that apparently if you get voice service through Comcast, you'll still need their combo modem unit of some sort. Well, cut that service from your monthly budget too. If we just had some competition, I'd cut Comcast out of my life completely.

Another thing is that if you have their modem and you need help with it, they may call it your responsibility and charge you for any "help" they provide. At least if you own your own stuff, you'll know if it's your problem or theirs.

Modem is straightforward and easy to use as any. If you ever download at high rates for days on end, it'll need cycled, but that's not the modem's fault; it just happens.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Cable Modem CM500 - Compatible with all Cable Providers incl. Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox | For Cable Plans up to 400Mbps | DOCSIS 3.0

text_fidelity_a:
Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10 You may know about the announcement from Lenovo a few weeks ago that going forward the company will be certifying all their ThinkPad and Thinkstation workstations for Linux. This computer is an IdeaCentre, not a ThinkPad or ThinkStation, and it comes preloaded with Windows, but I am a Linux user and I wanted to see if it will run Linux.

First things first: If you're looking for a gaming computer or something to handle graphics-intensive programs, this isn't it. It doesn't have a screaming fast processor, although it is a capable one. The onboard AMD Raven graphics module is pretty capable (I tried it out on a big display), but this model has no expansion slot for a video or audio card or any other such upgrades.

It does have a bay for a big 3.5 inch HDD with SATA connectors. And it comes with a 256GB SSD already installed on the motherboard. It also comes with 4GB RAM (and a second slot to add more), and a wired keyboard and mouse and the power supply. It has four USB 2.0 ports in the back, and two 2.0 and two 3.0 (gen 1) USB ports in the front. Also on the front are a card reader slot, the optical drive, mic and headset connection ports, and the power button. The back also has an HDMI port, VGA-out port, and and ethernet port.

It's about the size of an ITX mini tower form factor box, which is a little larger than a big dictionary. It stands upright, so the footprint is pretty small. And it's lightweight compared to a big desktop box.

I didn't even complete the first boot into Windows before attempting a Linux install. Tapping F2 on boot will get you into a graphical menu for picking your boot device, and F12 will get you into a deeper menu for selecting boot order and into the BIOS.

My favorite distro is Debian, so I thought I'd take a shot at installing it. It was a no-go. It didn't have the drivers for the onboard Atheros wifi card, and apparently a few other things. I actually pulled the wifi card off the motherboard and substituted a dongle and gave it a second try. I got Debian installed, but the machine still froze on boot without ever getting into the desktop environment.

So I tried installing Ubuntu, which, along with Red Hat, was specifically mentioned as now being supported by Lenovo. Success. Installation went smoothly. I was still using the dongle for wifi, so I shut down the machine and reinstalled the inboard card. Again, success. Wifi operated right away.

The couple of minor -- emphasizing minor -- things I don't like is that an inboard white LED glows continually when the power supply is plugged in, and as far as I can tell there's no way to turn it off.

Bottom line here is I think it's a good machine for general use. It's pretty capable, but be aware of its limitations so you won't be disappointed.
text_fidelity_b: Lenovo IdeaCentre 3 Desktop Tower, AMD Athlon Silver 3050U, AMD Radeon Graphics, 4GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, HDMI, Windows 10

Wi4You Recessed Wall Plate 2 Pack Decotive Cable Wall Plate with Fly Mounting Wings Bottom Opening for Low Voltage Cable Pass Through WI1009-2 I wanted a single-gang wall box so I could route pre-terminated Cat6 cables from behind my TV stand to my router in another room. Tired of the glitches you inherently get with wifi when running a FireTV stick 4K with a FireTV Recast so converted all to hardwired ethernet. System is much more responsive now and this product fit the bill. Comes in a 2 pack (one for each end), not expensive, easy to install, and comes with both the wall insert and a trim cover plate. Large opening at bottom inside the wall accommodates both Cat6 plug pass-thru, and multiple cables.

One note of caution: You obviously slide your plugs/cables through the box opening, then insert box into your wall cut-out, then tighten the 2 front screws which cause the flanges inside to flip around and clamp to the back side of your wall board. When tightening the bottom one, be sure none of your cables are trapped between the flange and wall. If so, you could pinch one or more cables.
